name: Hannya Mask
powers: Embodies a woman turned demon by jealousy
description: The hannya is a Noh theatre mask sculpted as the face of a woman transfigured by jealousy, resentment, or obsessive love into a horned, serpent-eyed demon with a gaping, fang-filled mouth and trailing metallic teeth. It is worn in plays such as Dojoji, where a spurned woman becomes a serpent that pursues the monk Anchin into a temple bell, and Aoi no Ue, where the living Rokujo no Miyasudokoro torments her rival through spirit-doctoring. The mask is carved in ascending grades of intensity, from a slightly raised mouth to a fully open jaw with gilded fangs, so a single hannya can move on stage from grief to pure fury. In the folk tradition the finished mask is treated with care because it is thought to retain the dangerous emotional charge it depicts, and carvers historically disposed of flawed examples ritually rather than letting them circulate. The hannya name is also used for the demon itself in the wider yokai lore that grew up around the Noh stage.

name: Oni no Kanabo
powers: Said to crush any demon or mortal it strikes
description: The kanabo is the iron-studded club that Japanese legend and art place in the grip of the oni, the ogre of the folk imagination, and it has become the oni's stock attribute to the point that the two are nearly inseparable in picture scrolls and festival prints. Tales from the Heian-era exploits of the demon queller Minamoto no Yorimitsu, above all his campaign against the bandit-ogre Shuten-doji, show the oni swinging the heavy mace with crushing force against heroes and their retainers; the same weapon appears in the folk tale of Momotaro, whose companions win against the ogres' island through wit. The club is conventionally imagined as a wooden shaft bound with iron hoops and studded with iron knobs, heavier than a man could lift, and it is treated as a mythological attribute rather than a documented artifact, since no original example survives. It carries real cultural weight, standing for brute strength that must be overcome by cleverness, and it remains the default prop of oni in the Setsubun bean-throwing rite and in modern manga and games.

name: Shimenawa
powers: Marks off divine ground and repels impurity
description: The shimenawa is the sacred rope twisted from rice straw that marks off the dwelling-place of the kami in Shinto practice, hung across the entrance of shrines, over torii gates, and around sacred trees, rocks, and rice paddies. Its origin is tied to the founding myth of the sun goddess Amaterasu, who sealed herself in the Heavenly Rock Cave and left the world in darkness until the other gods lured her out and strung a rope across the mouth of the cave to keep her from retreating again. The shimenawa draws a boundary between the purified ground of the kami and the defiling world outside, and its presence warns humans not to cross unbidden. It is braided from freshly harvested straw, in some regions hemp or straw hung with the paper streamers called shide, and the rope is renewed each year as part of New Year preparations at shrines across Japan. Larger examples, some spanning several metres, hang over the great torii of shrines such as Izumo Taisha and Fushimi Inari, making the rope one of the most visible symbols of Shinto itself.

name: Hagoromo
powers: Lets its wearer fly between heaven and earth
description: Hagoromo, the feather mantle, is the robe that lets a heavenly maiden, the tennyo, fly between the mortal world and the sky, and it is the central object of one of the most famous Noh plays, Hagoromo, set at Mio Bay. In the play a fisherman named Hakuryo finds a robe of feathers hanging from a pine and refuses to return it until the angel who owns it teaches him the dance of the moon palace, the promise of the robe's return drawing the divine world briefly into the human. The story belongs to the wider family of swan-maiden tales told across Eurasia, in which a supernatural woman loses her flying garment, marries a mortal, and departs when the garment is restored. In Japanese folklore the robe is woven from a thousand feathers and cannot be lifted by any ordinary hand, and a man who hides it may win the maiden's love but loses her when it is found. The play's theme of the boundary between human and divine, and the price of crossing it, has made the hagoromo a staple of Japanese literature and a name given to shrines and dance traditions honouring the heavenly maidens.
source: Noh play Hagoromo; coastal legend tradition

name: Kitsune's Crescent Comb
powers: Reveals a fox in human form; granting it service or love
description: The crescent-shaped comb of Japanese legend is the small hair ornament that a shapeshifting kitsune is said to drop when its disguise is betrayed, and finding it is supposed to bring a strange fortune or a lasting bond with the fox. The comb appears again and again in tales of fox wives, in which a man marries a beautiful woman who turns out to be a fox in human form; at the crucial moment the tail is seen, or the comb is left behind when the wife vanishes, and the discovery ends the marriage. In some variants the man who keeps the comb may command the fox's service or its gratitude, while in others the comb proves the spirit nature of the householder and drives the fox away for good. Because the fox in Japanese belief is both a trickster and a messenger of the rice god Inari, the comb carries an ambiguous charge: it is a clue, a keepsake, and a token of a crossing between the animal and human worlds. The motif is old enough to appear in the earliest collections of Japanese fox tales, and it still shapes modern retellings in which a comb on a shrine step promises a fox encounter.

name: Daruma Doll
powers: Talisman of perseverance and wish fulfillment
description: The daruma is a rounded paper-mache doll modelled on Bodhidharma, the semi-legendary founder of Zen Buddhism, whose hollow weighted body always rocks back upright when tipped. The likeness plays on a famous story in which Bodhidharma sat facing a wall in meditation for nine years, until his legs withered and were lost; the doll keeps his determined, round form and his fierce brow. Bought as a talisman of perseverance, the daruma is customarily sold with blank white eyes, and the owner inks in one eye when a wish or goal is set and the second when it is achieved, the rite turning the doll into a kind of visual contract with oneself. At the end of the year the accumulated daruma are taken to temples such as Dairyoji in Gunma, the dolls' birthplace, and burned in the daruma-kuyo ceremony, releasing the accumulated wishes. Originally a charm against smallpox in the Edo period, the doll has become a national symbol of resilience, famously adopted by political candidates, and its self-righting property gives the Japanese phrase 'falling seven times, rising eight' a concrete image.

name: Ruyi Jingu Bang
powers: Shrinks and grows at the wearer's will; weighs thirteen thousand five hundred catties
description: Ruyi Jingu Bang is the magic staff of Sun Wukong, the Monkey King of the great Chinese novel Journey to the West, and it is counted among the most famous weapons in all of Asian literature. The staff began as the great pillar of the Eastern Sea Dragon Palace, a golden-banded rod weighing thirteen thousand five hundred catties, which no one could lift until the Monkey King took it up and found it shrank and grew at his will, from a needle kept in his ear to a pillar that could reach the clouds. With it Sun Wukong defied the heavenly host, fought the armies of the Jade Emperor, and later escorted the monk Tripitaka to the West, the staff serving as both weapon and staff of office. The weapon's name is often translated as 'the complaisant golden cudgel' or 'wish-fulfilling staff,' and its image is inseparable from the character who wields it. Ruyi Jingu Bang appears throughout the sequel novel and in opera, film, and games, and remains the emblem of the irrepressible Monkey King.

name: Jiu Ding
powers: Signifies the Mandate of Heaven and legitimacy of rule
description: The jiu ding are the nine bronze tripods that the culture hero Yu the Great is said to have cast from tribute metal gathered across the Nine Provinces after he tamed the great flood, inscribing each region's creatures and things on the sides so that the people could recognize them. Passed down through the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties as the physical warrant of the Mandate of Heaven, they became the archetype of legitimate rule in Chinese historiography, and losing them was read as the fall of a dynasty. No actual ding survive, and their very existence is a matter of debate, but the story carried enormous political weight: Confucius, Mencius, and the historian Sima Qian all allude to the tripods as the vessels of sovereignty. In the Warring States tale of the King of Chu who 'asked about the tripods' at the Zhou court, the sheer idea of the ding became a test of ambition. The jiu ding remain the standard Chinese symbol of rightful imperial power and of the unity of the realm.

name: Hou Yi's Bow
powers: Shot down nine of the ten suns
description: The red bow of Hou Yi is the weapon of the legendary archer of Chinese myth who shot down nine of the ten suns that once scorched the earth, leaving a single sun to light the day. Each of the ten suns was the child of the goddess Xihe, and when all ten rose together the world began to burn; Hou Yi, a peerless bowman, felled nine of them with arrows tipped against the sun-birds that drew the solar chariot. In the same cycle of tales his skill earned him the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West, but his wife Chang'e swallowed it and drifted to the moon, and the archer was left behind. The bow therefore stands for the archetypal marksman and for the human cost of divine power, and Hou Yi is invoked across Chinese literature whenever perfect archery is described. The tale, recorded in Han-era sources and echoed in the poem 'Tianwen', gives the bow a permanent place among the weapons of Chinese mythology.

name: Elixir of Immortality
powers: Bestows eternal life
description: The elixir of immortality is the drug of eternal life that the Queen Mother of the West, Xiwangmu, is said to have kept in her paradise of Kunlun, and it is the pivot of one of the most famous tales in Chinese mythology. The archer Hou Yi obtained the elixir as a reward for shooting down the nine suns, but his wife Chang'e swallowed it to keep it from a thief, and was lifted to the moon where she lives forever in the cold lunar palace. The tale, recorded in Han-era sources such as Huainanzi, gave the moon its goddess, and the jade rabbit that pounds herbs in a mortar is her companion on the lunar surface. In later Daoist tradition the elixir became the goal of alchemy, both as a physical drug of cinnabar and gold and as an inner refinement of the body's energies. The story anchors the Mid-Autumn Festival, when offerings of mooncakes recall Chang'e's flight, and the elixir remains the standard image of the Daoist quest for transcendence.

name: Jade Rabbit's Mortar
powers: Pounds the elixir of immortality
description: The mortar and pestle with which the Jade Rabbit pounds the elixir of immortality is a fixed image in the Chinese moon, the rabbit standing beside the cassia tree on the lunar surface as the companion of the goddess Chang'e. In the Moon Rabbit folklore, the rabbit first earned its place when it offered itself as food to a disguised deity, who spared it and set it on the moon to grind the herbs of immortality, and the same moon-rabbit motif recurs across East Asian lore. In Korea the rabbit is said to pound the ingredients of the rice cake tteok, while in Japan it pounds mochi, and in Vietnam it is the companion of the moon goddess Hang Nga. The mortar is depicted in Mid-Autumn Festival imagery on lanterns, mooncakes, and shadow-puppets, and the figure of the rabbit at work is one of the most recognizable of the moon's markings. Across all these traditions the mortar turns the mundane labour of grinding grain into the cosmic work of producing the elixir of life.
source: Han bronze mirrors and moon-rabbit tradition

name: Bagua Mirror
powers: Deflects harmful energy (sha qi) and returns evil glances
description: The bagua mirror is a circular mirror ringed with the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes around a central yin-yang disc, hung over doorways in Chinese feng shui practice to turn away harmful energy, sha qi, and to return an attacker's evil gaze. In domestic use it is placed above the main door or facing a threatening structure such as a road, a corner, or a neighbour's roof-ridge, so that the mirror deflects or reflects the influence back to its source. The mirror also appears in Daoist talismanic practice, paired with written spells against hauntings and possession, and the convex form is said to disperse harm while the concave form gathers or focuses it. Because of its power to reflect, the bagua mirror is one of the few feng shui remedies that practitioners advise using with care, lest the mirrored effect fall on an innocent. The object joins the practical science of geomancy to the older Chinese belief in mirrors as revealers of spirits, a connection that goes back to the bronze mirrors of the Han period.

name: Guan Dao
material: Steel blade on a long wooden shaft
powers: Emblem of martial protection and the god of war
description: The guan dao is the heavy curved-blade polearm historically associated with Guan Yu, the great general of the Three Kingdoms period who was deified as the god of war and of righteousness, and its most famous example is the Green Dragon Crescent Blade. In Romance of the Three Kingdoms Guan Yu carries the enormous weapon, and in legend the blade was so heavy that only he could wield it; temples honouring him display a ceremonial guan dao in his image, and the weapon became a standard of the military temples and of martial artists. The actual historical guan dao developed later than the general's lifetime, and the famous blade is a literary creation, but the association made the weapon a fixture of Chinese and East Asian iconography. In the folk tradition a guan dao kept in a home or temple is thought to carry Guan Yu's protective presence, and it is still carried in lion-dance performances and temple processions. The blade's name has passed into popular culture across the world as the emblem of the bearded warrior-saint.

name: Flaming Pearl
powers: Signifies wisdom, wealth, and transformation
description: The flaming pearl, huozhu, is a luminous orb wreathed in curling flame that Chinese art shows two dragons chasing or guarding, and it is one of the most common motifs of East Asian decoration. The image appears on temple roofs, ceramic dishes, paintings, and lanterns, and its meaning draws on several layers: in Buddhist iconography the pearl is the cintamani, the wish-granting jewel that fulfils every desire, while in Daoist cosmology it can stand for the moon, the sun, or the inner pearl of spiritual refinement. The dragon that guards the pearl is usually the celestial dragon of rain and water, and the chase motif is sometimes read as the play of yin and yang or of the sun and moon across the heavens. In folk belief the pearl is also linked to the treasure of the dragon's undersea palace, and stories tell of heroes who descend to the sea king's court for the jewel. Whatever the reading, the flaming pearl carries a consistent charge of wisdom, wealth, and transformation, and it remains the standard companion of the dragon in pan-Asian art.
source: Dragon art motif; Buddhist jewel tradition

name: The Heavenly Loom
powers: Wove the patterned clouds of the sky
description: The heavenly loom is the celestial weaving frame of Zhinü, the Weaver Girl, who in Chinese myth wove the patterned clouds of the sky beside the Heavenly River, the Milky Way. When she married the cowherd Niulang and neglected her weaving, the Jade Emperor or the Queen Mother of the West separated the pair across the river, allowing them to meet only once a year; on the seventh night of the seventh month, magpies form a bridge over the river and the lovers reunite. The tale, first recorded in Han-era poetry, became the origin of the Qixi festival, the Chinese Valentine's day, when girls pray to Zhinü for skill in needlework and for love. The loom is thus the engine of the sky's patterned beauty and the emblem of the craft that the festival celebrates. The same story is told in Korea as Chilseok and in Japan as Tanabata, where the weaving goddess Orihime is remembered with strips of paper hung on bamboo.
source: Qixi legend; Han to Tang sources

name: Cheonbuin
powers: Marks the royal mandate of the founder king
description: The cheonbuin, the heavenly seal, is the seal that the Samguk Yusa says Hwanung, son of the sky god Hwanin, carried when he descended to Mount Taebaek with three seals to govern the world. In the Dangun foundation myth Hwanung established a sacred city at the summit, legislated for the people, and accepted the prayers of a bear and a tiger who wished to become human; the bear that endured the ordeal of a hundred days in a cave became the woman Ungnyeo, whose son Dangun founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon. The seal is given to the king's descendants as the mark of royal mandate, anchoring Korean sovereignty in the descent of the royal line from heaven. The story is recorded in the Samguk Yusa and the Jewang Ungi, and it is the foundational myth of Korean identity, celebrated in the founding day festival of Gaecheonjeol. The cheonbuin is often paired in royal regalia with the sword of office, and the image of Hwanung descending with the seal is a fixed scene in Korean national symbolism.

name: Geobukseon
powers: Iron-roofed warship that shed fire and boarding parties
description: The geobukseon, the turtle ship, is the armoured warship that Admiral Yi Sun-sin built for the Korean fleet in the 1590s to repel the Japanese invasions of the Imjin War, and it is the most celebrated naval vessel in Korean history. The ship was roofed with an iron-studded shell that shed fire arrows and repelled boarding parties, and it was fitted with cannon that could be fired from the sides while the deck stayed protected. Although the turtle ship was a real and effective warship, it passed quickly into folklore as an invincible protector of the coast, celebrated in songs, tales, and the war memoirs of Admiral Yi himself. Modern scholarship notes that the historical vessels were smaller and less dramatic than later depictions, but the legend endures, and the turtle ship is a national symbol of defence and ingenuity. Reconstructions are displayed and sailed at memorials such as the Hyeonchungsa shrine and the war museum in Seoul, and the turtle ship remains the emblem of Korean naval power.

name: Gogok
powers: Symbol of rank, fertility, and the sun
description: The gogok is the comma-shaped jade ornament threaded onto the gold crowns, belts, and necklaces of the ancient Silla kingdom, excavated in large numbers from the tombs of Gyeongju, and it is the most distinctive form of Korean prehistoric jade. Carved from hard nephrite and often pale green or white, the beads may derive from the shamanic curved beads of the north and are linked by scholars to fertility symbolism and to the bear-woman Ungnyeo's offering in the Dangun foundation myth. In the tombs of Silla's elite the gogok hangs from the crowns and diadems in cascading rows, and the form persisted into the Gaya and Baekje kingdoms. Modern Korean scholarship sees in the curved bead an image of a claw or a moon-crescent, and the gogok appears on the national emblem of the modern Gyeongju region. It remains the emblem of ancient Korean royal regalia and one of the most recognizable objects of the country's archaeological heritage.

name: Bangmangi
powers: Grants whatever the wielder wishes when struck
description: The bangmangi is the magic club of the dokkaebi, the mischievous goblin of Korean folklore, which grants whatever a person wishes when it is struck. In the folktales the dokkaebi owns the club and uses it to summon food, gold, and servants, and clever humans trick the gullible goblin into surrendering it: a thief or a poor man persuades the dokkaebi that a beating with the club will bring a blessing, then runs off with the prize. In other variants the club is swapped, or its possessor uses it to draw endless rice and healing, and the object is so tied to its owner that the dokkaebi and its bangmangi are nearly interchangeable in stories. The club appears in the collected Korean tales of Im Bang and Yi Ryuk and in the oral tradition of the pansori storytellers, and it remains a beloved fixture of Korean children's literature and animation. The bangmangi embodies the dokkaebi's double nature as both threat and source of luck.

name: Thuan Thien Sword
powers: Granted victory over the Ming invaders
description: Thuan Thien, the Sword of Heaven's Will, is the magic blade given to the farmer-king Le Loi during his revolt against the Ming occupation of Dai Viet in the fifteenth century, when the golden turtle god Kim Qui surfaced from the waters to present it. With the sword Le Loi's army defeated the Ming and he founded the Later Le dynasty, ruling as the national hero of Vietnamese independence. After the victory, when the king was boating on the lake in Hanoi, the great turtle rose again and seized the sword, returning it to its divine owner, and the lake was renamed Hoan Kiem, the Lake of the Returned Sword. The story is told in the fifteenth-century Lam Son thuc luc chronicle and is a centrepiece of Vietnamese national identity, and the island pagoda Ngoc Son on the lake commemorates the event. Thuan Thien is also celebrated in the legend of the turtle that bore the sword, and the blade remains the emblem of Vietnam's struggle for independence.

name: Betel and Areca Tray
powers: Foundation of hospitality and marriage ritual
description: The betel and areca tray is the lacquered brass container that carries betel leaves, areca nut, and lime, the essential offering of Vietnamese hospitality, courtship, and marriage ritual. In the founding legend two twin brothers, Cao and Lang, loved the same woman; when the woman married Cao, Lang wandered away and died by a stream, and Cao, grieving, drowned himself; the woman then died too. The gods transformed the brothers into the areca tree and the betel vine that climbs it, and the woman into the limestone that binds their flavour, so that the chewing of betel and areca joins the three together in eternal kinship. The tray is presented at weddings as a symbol of this bond, offered to guests as a mark of respect, and placed before ancestors during rites. In village custom the exchange of betel seals a promise, and the phrase 'to invite betel' still means to ask for a daughter's hand. The tray is among the most symbolic household objects of Vietnamese culture.
source: Betel and areca legend; folk custom

name: The Jade Emperor's Gong
powers: Summoned rain when struck by the frog
description: The Jade Emperor's gong is the bronze instrument of a Vietnamese folk tale in which a frog leads a deputation of animals to heaven to complain that rain never falls. Because the frog croaks so loudly, the Jade Emperor hears it above the clouds and summons the delegation; the frog is granted the power to control rain, and to this day the croaking of frogs is said to warn of coming rain. In some tellings the frog beats the Jade Emperor's own bronze gong to announce the arrival of the animals, or to wake the sleepy god, and the tale survives chiefly through oral retellings across the Red River delta. The gong is a story element rather than a documented artifact, and it belongs to the large Vietnamese cycle of pourquoi tales about the order of the natural world. The story explains both the frog's croak and the dragon's water-taming work, and it is one of the most retold animal tales in the Vietnamese classroom.

name: Co Loa Crossbow
powers: Each shot could slay thousands
description: The magic crossbow of Co Loa is the weapon of An Duong Vuong, the legendary king of the Au Lac kingdom, whose trigger was forged from the golden claw of Kim Qui, the golden turtle god, and which could kill thousands of men with a single shot. The king built the spiral citadel of Co Loa with the turtle's help, but his defence was undone by his own daughter: My Chau, newly married to the spy Trong Thuy of the northern enemy, showed him the secret of the trigger, and the enemy stole it, the citadel fell, and An Duong Vuong fled with his daughter. Learning of the betrayal, the king beheaded My Chau, and her blood is said to have turned into pearls. The story is told in the Lĩnh Nam chích quái and the Dai Viet su ky toan thu, and it is one of the foundational legends of Vietnamese national memory, the site at Co Loa near Hanoi being among the oldest archaeological monuments of the country.

name: The Emerald Buddha's Robes
aliases: Royal Vestments of the Emerald Buddha
powers: Palladium of the Thai kingdom
description: The three robes of gold worn by the Emerald Buddha are the seasonal garments changed on the sacred image in the Wat Phra Kaew, the Temple of the Emerald Buddha in Bangkok, in a ceremony performed by the king. The image, carved from a single block of jade, sits above the golden pedestal in the royal chapel, and its vestments are swapped three times a year, at the start of the hot, rainy, and cool seasons, in a rite that binds the monarchy to the welfare of the realm. The robes themselves are made of gold cloth and jewelled ornaments, and their alternation is fixed by royal ritual. The image's long history, moving through Laos and Cambodia before being enshrined in Bangkok, is told as the palladium of the Thai state, the object whose possession legitimized the kingdom. The Emerald Buddha and its robes are the axis of Thai national and religious identity, and the ceremony draws crowds whenever the garments are changed.

name: The Naga's Jewel
powers: Grants wealth and kingship to its holder
description: The jewel of the naga is the luminous gem that the great serpent of the Mekong, the naga, is said to guard in its watery underworld palace, and that grants wealth, kingship, or the fulfilment of wishes to whoever obtains it. In Thai and Lao river lore the naga is the protector of the river and of the people who live along it, and the jewel is sometimes linked to the fireballs that rise from the water during the full-moon festival of the eleventh lunar month, when the naga is said to breathe fire in celebration. The motif echoes the wider South and Southeast Asian image of the naga as the keeper of the earth's hidden treasure, and the jewel recurs in tales of kings who win the naga's favour. Because the naga is both a guardian and a dangerous boundary-keeper, the jewel is a reward for courage or reverence and a fatal prize for greed. The legend is retold across the Mekong and its tributaries, binding the serpent to the geography of the river.

name: The Bayon Smile
powers: The king's watchful presence over the kingdom
description: The Bayon smile is the serene, downcast smile of the great stone face-towers of the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom, built in the twelfth century under the Buddhist king Jayavarman VII. Scores of colossal faces, each several metres high, gaze from the four sides of the towers, and scholars debate whether they portray the king himself, the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, or the fusion of the two in the king's consecrated image. Khmer legend and local tradition read the many faces as the king's presence watching over his kingdom from every direction, a gaze both compassionate and sovereign. The temple was the state temple of Jayavarman's capital, and its face-towers combine Mahayana Buddhist devotion with the Khmer tradition of the devaraja, the god-king. The Bayon smile has become the emblem of Angkor and of Cambodian identity, appearing on the national flag and in art worldwide as an image of serene royal power.

name: The Four White Umbrellas
powers: Emblems of the right to rule granted from above
description: The four white umbrellas are the tiered white standards that the Burmese chronicles place among the regalia of the first kings of the Bagan and later dynasties, emblems of the right to rule granted from above. In the creation tale of kingship, the story of Thagya Min and the first king, the white umbrella is the mark of the king chosen by heaven, and the number of umbrellas carried over a ruler marked his rank, with the great white umbrella of the king symbolizing the highest authority. The image of the king as the bearer of the white umbrella survives in the Hmannan Yazawin chronicle and in the coronation imagery of the Burmese court, and the umbrella standard still crowns Burmese pagodas and throne halls as marks of sacred authority. The same iconography is shared with Thailand and Laos, where the tiered white parasol is the emblem of the Buddhist king. The four umbrellas bind earthly sovereignty to the blessing of the nats, the spirits who watch over the realm.

name: The Relic of That Phanom
powers: Focus of veneration; guardian presence of the Mekong
description: The relic of That Phanom is a sacred relic of the Buddha's breastbone enshrined in the great stupa of That Phanom on the Mekong, the most revered chedi of Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao legend holds that two monks carried the relic to the site and that a naga king, Phanya Sithan, invited the company and guarded the shrine, binding the sacred monument to the serpentine protectors of the river; the date of the enshrinement is given as the Year of the Goat and celebrated every year at the That Phanom festival. The stupa itself, a tall pyramidal chedi gilded in gold, was severely damaged by a storm in 1975 and rebuilt with a national campaign, and it remains a pilgrimage centre drawing people from both banks of the Mekong. The relic is venerated as a palladium of the region, and its festival in the twelfth lunar month, the Bun Pha That Phanom, is one of the great gatherings of Lao Buddhism. The connection of the shrine to the naga reflects the deep riverine religion of the Mekong valley.

name: Khaen
powers: Voice of lam song and festival celebration
description: The khaen is the free-reed mouth organ of Laos, built from rows of bamboo tubes bound around a wooden wind-chest, whose drone-and-melody sound is the soul of the Lao folk song called lam. The player breathes in and out through a single mouth-hole while covering the finger-holes of the tubes, producing the interlocking melody and drone that lam singers improvise against, and the instrument accompanies courtship, festivals, and ritual across Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao tradition says that the khaen shaped the speech and poetry of the people, and the instrument is central to the great courtship tradition of the khap and lam. In the origin legend the khaen was first made by a man who wanted to imitate the sound of the wind in the bamboo, and its seven-note scale is regarded as the seed of Lao musical thought. UNESCO has inscribed the khaen playing of the Lao people as intangible cultural heritage, and the instrument remains the emblem of Lao national music.

name: The Golden Whip of Genghis Khan
powers: Said to rally and reward warriors of the khan
description: The golden whip of Genghis Khan is the legendary whip that the great conqueror is said to have carried and brandished to rally and reward his warriors, and in some tellings the source of his military genius. One of the most retold stories claims that Genghis Khan rode with a whip made of gold that he used to command his armies, and that its mere sight could turn a retreat into a charge. No such whip survives, and the Secret History of the Mongols does not name it; the golden whip appears instead in later heroic retellings and in the popular narrative that grew around the conqueror's rise. The object is thus best understood as a modern legend rather than a documented relic, and its currency reflects the way Genghis Khan has been reimagined as a national and pan-Asian hero. The golden whip nevertheless appears in monuments and museums, and it stands for the charismatic authority by which the steppe armies were held together.

name: The Whistling Arrow
powers: Signal whistle that directed cavalry maneuvers
description: The whistling arrow is the signal arrow of the Mongol armies, tipped with a drilled bone or wooden head that shrieked in flight, and it was used by Genghis Khan's cavalry to direct charges, ambushes, and encirclements across the steppe. Described by Persian chroniclers such as Juvaini and by Chinese observers, the arrow worked by sound rather than by wounding: the drilled head, often globular with holes, screamed as it flew, and the direction and number of whistles could carry simple commands to units spread across the plain. The technology descended from the signal arrows of the earlier steppe peoples, and it allowed the tightly coordinated movements that made the Mongol armies so formidable. The whistle is also associated with hunting and with the signals of the ordo, the ruler's camp. The whistling arrow survives as a motif of the swift, coordinated warfare that built the empire, and reproductions are made for museums and festivals.
source: Persian and Chinese chronicles of the Mongol campaigns

name: Morin Khuur
powers: Voice of the horse and the steppe
description: The morin khuur, the horse-head fiddle, is the two-stringed instrument of Mongolia whose scroll is carved as a horse's head, whose strings and bow are of horsehair, and whose sound is held to imitate the breath and song of the horse. The classic origin legend tells of a herdsman whose beloved horse was killed by a treacherous lord; from the horse's skull, skin, mane, and tail the man made the first fiddle, so that the animal's spirit would sing on. The instrument carries a deep spiritual charge: it is played in homes, at ceremonies, and at the Naadam festival, and traditional players observed taboos in its presence, regarding it as a living being. In the twentieth century the morin khuur was adopted as the national instrument of Mongolia and inscribed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. Its two strings are often described as the two poles of Mongol identity, and the instrument is taught, collected, and displayed as the emblem of Mongolian national culture.

name: Tsagaan Tug
powers: Ensign of khanly authority and national unity
description: The tsagaan tug, the white standard, is the ensign of Genghis Khan's lineage that Mongol tradition honours as the sacred symbol of the khagan's authority, kept at the mausoleum complex in Ordos and paraded at the Naadam festival together with the nine black banners. The standard is a spear shaft crowned with a horsehair tuft or a looped top, and its white colour links it to the heavenly realm, the midday sun, and peace, while the nine black standards of the great khan stood for war and the nine tribes of the Mongols. In Mongol belief the tug is an object of reverence in its own right, and the ceremony of raising and lowering it is attended by ritual and by the offering of airag, fermented mare's milk. The white standard is central to the cult of Genghis Khan that survives among the Ordos Mongols, who preserve his relics in the mausoleum. The tug remains the emblem of the steppe khans and of Mongolian sovereignty.

name: Phurba
powers: Pins down demons during exorcism rituals
description: The phurba is the three-sided ritual dagger of Tibetan Buddhism, whose pommel is carved with the head of a wrathful deity such as Vajrakilaya and whose triangular blade is meant to pin down demonic forces at the boundary between the worlds. Used by lamas in exorcism and meditation rituals, the phurba transfixes evil like a tent-peg, and in the rituals of the Nyingma school it is treated as the vehicle of the deity Vajrakilaya himself. The dagger is made of iron, brass, or wood, and inscribed and consecrated examples survive in temple collections; some are old weapons pressed into ritual service, while others were made purely for the rite. The practitioner drives the phurba into earth, sand, or the image of a demon, and its three edges symbolize the transformation of the three poisons of the mind. Beyond ritual use, the phurba has become one of the most collected and reproduced objects of Himalayan art, and it is displayed in museums worldwide as an emblem of Tibetan Buddhist power.
source: Tibetan tantric ritual tradition; temple collections

name: Prayer Wheel
material: Metal and wood over a paper scroll
powers: Releases mantra prayers with each turn
description: The prayer-wheel is the cylindrical device of Tibetan Buddhism that is spun to release the mantras printed on the paper scrolls inside, each revolution sending the prayer for compassion into the world. Rows of large wheels line the walls of temples and stupas, and smaller hand-held wheels are turned by pilgrims at shrines and along circumambulation paths, the turning of the wheel standing for the turning of the dharma. The practice descends from the Indian and Tibetan tradition of reading or rolling sacred verses, and the mantra most often printed inside is Om Mani Padme Hum, the invocation of the bodhisattva of compassion Avalokiteshvara. Devout practitioners regard the wheel as a powerful means of accumulating merit for all beings, and it is customarily turned clockwise with the right hand while walking a clockwise circuit. The prayer-wheel has become a universal emblem of Tibetan Buddhism, and it appears in art and objects made for pilgrims across the Himalayan world.

name: Yeouiju
powers: Grants wishes; lets the imugi become a dragon
description: The yeouiju is the wish-granting jewel of Korean lore, the glowing orb that a serpent, imugi, must grasp to climb into full dragonhood, and that grants any wish to its holder. In the tales the imugi, a hornless dragon, waits for the jewel to fall from the sky or to be revealed by a righteous person, and the story of the imugi that lost the jewel at the waterfall is among the most famous Korean dragon tales. The yeouiju is also described as the possession of the dragon kings of the sea and of the mountain spirits, and its power is sometimes linked to the moon, whose light it is said to drink. In Buddhist-influenced versions the jewel is identified with the cintamani, the wish-fulfilling gem, and in shamanic tradition it is a shaman's treasure. The yeouiju appears in the imagery of the dokkaebi goblin as well, and it remains one of the most evocative objects of Korean mythic symbolism, standing for the attainment of the unattainable.

name: Macuahuitl
material: Wooden club edged with obsidian blades
powers: Slices through flesh in a single stroke; a mark of warrior rank.
description: The macuahuitl is the flat wooden sword edged with rows of razor-sharp obsidian blades that was the signature weapon of Aztec and Mesoamerican warriors at the time of the Spanish conquest. Chroniclers including Bernal Diaz describe its edge as sharp enough to behead a horse with a single stroke, and the codices and tribute lists record it as both a weapon of war and a mark of rank, with captured enemies often carrying the most ornate examples. The weapon was made of a wooden paddle, in some examples the paddle slotted and the blades set in, and obsidian edges were renewed as they dulled. The macuahuitl belonged to the wider Mesoamerican tradition of the maquahuitl and the atlatl, and it was used by elite warriors such as the jaguar and eagle knights. After the conquest the weapon passed quickly into legend, and no complete original survives, but it remains the most iconic weapon of the Aztec empire.
source: Conquistador chronicles (e.g. Bernal Díaz del Castillo)

name: Atlatl
material: Carved wood with antler or bone spur
powers: Hurls a dart with far greater force than an unaided arm.
description: The atlatl is the carved wooden spear-thrower that hurls darts with far greater force than an unaided arm, used across Mesoamerica from the Olmec era through the Aztec empire and beyond. Spanish accounts and Aztec codices show warriors and hunters gripping the notched end of the thrower while the dart rests in its socket, and its power is credited with punching through the cotton armour and even the mail of the Spanish at short range. The atlatl was also a ritual object: the great Aztec festivals included darts thrown in honour of the gods, and the weapon appears in the hand of deities such as Huitzilopochtli in the codices. The thrower was made of hard wood, sometimes decorated with shell and turquoise, and the socket that fits the dart's butt allowed the lever to add speed and reach. The atlatl survived in the New World long after it fell out of use elsewhere, and it is the ancestor of the spear-throwing devices of the Americas.
source: Florentine Codex and early Spanish accounts

name: Xiuhuitzolli
material: Wood frame covered in turquoise mosaic
powers: Sign of divine kingship; only the tlatoani may wear it.
description: The xiuhuitzolli is the pointed diadem of turquoise mosaic worn by the Aztec tlatoque, the supreme rulers, as the emblem of sovereignty, its name meaning 'pointed thing of turquoise.' The right to wear it was held to come from the gods and to pass with the kingship, and colonial accounts record that the ruler Motecuhzoma was crowned with one at his accession. The Codex Mendoza and the Florentine Codex show the crown above a headband of the same mosaic, and the turquoise itself was a material charged with solar and divine significance, gathered through long-distance trade and set by master lapidaries. The xiuhuitzolli was one element of a full regalia that included the nose-piece, ear-plugs, and the royal cloak, and its loss at the conquest was read as the end of legitimate Aztec rule. Surviving turquoise mosaic crowns and their fragments are among the most treasured objects of the museums of Mexico and Europe, and the diadem remains the icon of Aztec sovereignty.

name: Ehecailacacozcatl
powers: Command of the wind that sweeps the road before the rain gods.
description: The ehecailacacozcatl, the 'wind jewel,' is the spiral shell breast ornament of the wind god Quetzalcoatl in his aspect of Ehecatl, worn at the throat and tied to the whirlwind that sweeps the road before the rain god Tlaloc and scatters the seeds of the world. Aztec images of Quetzalcoatl-Ehecatl show the cut conch worn as a pectoral and the spiral shell among his emblems, and the Florentine Codex connects the wind god's journeys to the clearing of the rain's path. The shell is the conch of the wind, its spiral echoing the whirlwind and its sound carrying the breath of the god, and the ornament is sometimes paired with the crown of feathers of the wind god's dancing form. The ehecailacacozcatl belongs to the larger Mesoamerican symbolism of the conch as music, rain, and fertility. It is one of the defining attributes of Ehecatl in Aztec and earlier Teotihuacan art, and it remains a standard emblem of the wind deity in studies of Mesoamerican religion.
